title: Who may say I am Brahman?
hookLine: Brahman says it first; then anyone who wakes may
carry: whoever wakes to Brahman may say it
tomorrow: aham, brahma, asmi: three little words. which one does the work?
last: WHAT'S INNERMOST CAN'T BE LEFT BEHIND.

lines: WHO GETS TO SAY I AM?
cards: A card tucked into a bag by someone who isn't family but almost is, with a verse written inside. Old words travel like that, hand to hand. So, one question today: who gets to say I am, and mean it all the way down?
The Brihadaranyaka has an answer. A neighbor tradition has one too, and its answer starts at a burning bush.

teach.b: Here's the sentence this week is named for. In the beginning this was Brahman, and it knew itself only: I am Brahman. Aham brahmasmi.
So it became all. Then the text opens the door.
Whoever among the gods woke up to this became that; so too among the sages; so too among people.

teach.h: EXODUS: I AM THAT I AM.
teach.b: Even the gods can't stop such a person, it adds, because that person becomes their very self.

teach.h: GOD'S OWN NAME, OR SAID BY A KNOWER.
teach.b: In the Hebrew Bible, Moses stands before a bush that burns and isn't burned up, and asks God's name.
In the King James Version the answer is: "I AM THAT I AM: and he said, Thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel, I AM hath sent me unto you." Here's what the two share.
At the deepest point, both reach for the plainest words there are: I am. Not a title, not a list. Being, said in the first person.

And here's the honest difference. In Exodus, I AM is God's own name, spoken to Moses. Moses carries it to his people; he doesn't say it of himself, and Jewish and Christian teaching keep God and the person distinct.

In the Brihadaranyaka, Brahman says it first, and then it's opened to whoever wakes: as Advaita hears it, a person may say it of their own deepest self; as other Vedanta schools hear it, of the Brahman dwelling within.

teach.h: TWO DOORS, ONE PLAIN I AM.
teach.b: The same plain words, two different doors.

how: In Vedanta, aham brahmasmi is studied in its Brihadaranyaka setting and read differently by each school; Exodus 3:14 is read by Jews and Christians as God revealing the divine name to Moses.

o: I am sent: a messenger's opening words
I am new: a vow made at a fresh start
I am Brahman: the self is the one reality

games.q: who says I am? tap the pairs.
p: said first by Brahman, knowing itself
God's own name, or opened to knowers

s: the Brihadaranyaka says only Brahman may ever say aham brahmasmi
whoever among the gods, sages and people woke up to it became that.
in Exodus, I AM THAT I AM is the answer when Moses asks God's name
Exodus 3:14, in the King James Version.
Exodus and the Brihadaranyaka teach exactly the same idea
both reach for 'I am'; in Exodus it's God's own name, and God and Moses stay distinct.

games.q: a classmate says: 'Moses and the Upanishad both said they were God.' you've just read both texts. what's fair?
o: Exodus gives I AM as God's name to Moses; the Upanishad opens it to knowers.
agree: both texts say each person is God, word for word.
disagree: neither text uses the words 'I am' at all.
games.why: in Exodus, I AM is God's name; Moses carries it, he doesn't claim it. in the Brihadaranyaka, whoever wakes to aham brahmasmi becomes that. close words, honestly different.

practice: Sit tall, both feet on the floor, hands open on your knees. With each out-breath, let only the two plainest words rest in the mind: I am. No name after them.
Stay with those two words and the breath that carries them.

wordCard.voice: Aham brahmasmi: I am Brahman, said first by Brahman knowing itself, then opened to whoever wakes to it.

orig.note: Sanskrit asmi, am: the last word of aham brahmasmi, joined to brahma when spoken.

carryVoice: Keep this one: whoever wakes to Brahman may say it, I am Brahman. Day 1749 is done.

sources.ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 1.4.10 (in the beginning this was Brahman; it knew itself only: I am Brahman; so it became all; whoever among the gods, sages or people awoke to it became that; even the gods cannot prevent it, for he becomes their self)
Exodus 3:2 (the bush burned with fire and was not consumed)
